source_terms: Within the format, alignments between elements create structure.
space is divided based on content: like information is grouped together, disparate information is separated; their resulting widths and heights subdivide the surrounding field
item.claim: Structure arises from the content, not the other way round. Like information is grouped and disparate information separated; the widths and heights those groups occupy are what subdivide the surrounding field. A grouping may yield a single axis dividing the space into two fields, or many axes and correspondingly complex subdivisions. Changes in weight and scale introduce hierarchy — the source's word for visual ordering — to the information.

mechanism.text: Grouping and separating produce edges; the edges are alignments; the alignments are the structure. The demonstration holds content constant and varies only the grouping.

scope.conditions: any composition of mixed information within a format

caveats.text: the source notes both demonstrated compositions use the same type family and only a selection of possible sizes, so an enormous variety of layouts is reachable within strict limitations
this is the section's clearest controlled comparison, but it is a designed illustration rather than a test — no claim is made about what a viewer does with either version

positive.description: same event poster set two ways, each shown beside the alignment structure it implies: a two-field division and a multi-field grid

intra_source_relations.note: the reciprocity of content and structure is argued at length later

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
item.question: A key label in a dense, structureless poster is partly obscured. A colleague proposes repeating it in a clear area of the page. What does Samara say about that move, and what does he prefer?
item.answer: He allows it and then withdraws most of the allowance. Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help, he says, but it may also confuse a viewer with its redundancy — better to give the information a little extra room where it appears in sequence. So his preference is to fix the element in place rather than duplicate it. He pairs this with a general fallback: when in doubt, simplify, because if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, the element will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.
item.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": repetition of obscured information may help or may confuse through redundancy, with extra room in sequence preferred; and the when-in-doubt-simplify rule with its reason.
confounders: treating repetition as a straightforwardly safe redundancy strategy
assuming the fix is to increase the label's size, which is a different lever in his account
confusing this repetition with the repetition he recommends elsewhere, which marks which elements are alike in meaning

item.visible_content: Four panels in two rows. Left of each row, a poster for the same event — a Hear-Say reading by Henry Magaziner at a Philadelphia bookshop, with the same date, time and address. Right of each row, the alignment structure that composition implies, drawn as teal rules. Top row: the information is set as one flush-right stack, and the derived structure is two fields divided by a single vertical axis. Bottom row: the same information is broken into several differently-weighted groups scattered across the format, and the derived structure is a multi-field grid of roughly five vertical and five horizontal divisions.
item.what_the_visual_supports: That a grid is READ OFF a composition rather than imposed on it. The content is held constant and only the grouping changes, and the structure changes with it. It also supports the source's narrower claim that a large variety of layouts is reachable inside strict limits: both posters use one type family and a small set of sizes.
item.requires_prose: That like information is grouped and disparate information separated, and that changes in weight and scale are what introduce hierarchy. The picture shows the outcome; the caption supplies the rule that produced it.
item.extractor_note: This is the clearest minimal pair in the section — same content, one variable (grouping) changed, both results shown with their derived structures. The caption states the claim, so a text-only extraction keeps the claim and loses the proof.

source_terms:
Bigger and bolder usually means "seen first," so applying such differences to greater extremes than one normally would is a useful strategy.
Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help, but it may also confuse a viewer with its redundancy—better to give it a little extra room where it appears in sequence.
When in doubt, simplify: if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, it will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.
item.claim: Ensuring that a reader can easily identify the most important elements, or those from which a sequence originates, is critical. Because bigger and bolder usually means seen first, the source's remedy for an unusual composition is not a different device but the same device applied to greater extremes than one normally would. Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help but may also confuse the viewer with its redundancy; the source prefers giving that information a little extra room where it already appears in the sequence. Where doubt remains, simplify — if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, it will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.

mechanism.text: Differentiation is relative to its field. A complicated field raises the threshold, so the contrast that would suffice in a quiet layout has to be increased, or the field simplified, for the same element to read as first.

scope.conditions: alternative layouts, where the surrounding field is optically busy

caveats.text: "Greater extremes than one normally would" is comparative with no anchor. The source gives no magnitude and no way to know when the exaggeration has become the new normal.
Repetition of obscured information is offered and withdrawn in the same sentence, so the source's own position on it is a preference rather than a rule.

source_stated_problems: redundancy from repeating partially obscured information may confuse a viewer
source_stated_remedies: apply size and weight differences to greater extremes than usual
give partially obscured information extra room where it appears in sequence rather than repeating it elsewhere
when in doubt, simplify — fewer elements or less interference

intra_source_relations.note: the optical differentiation half of the diagnosis

source_terms:
Imagery as a Source
what happens if the visual aspects of imagery are allowed to rule, so to speak—to determine not only the compositional structure of a project overall, but the compositional and stylistic attributes of the type?
Typography is always a pattern of lines, but images present a radically greater range of form languages
item.claim: Bringing type and image together is described as notoriously difficult because each has formal characteristics most often at odds with the other, and because the two are usually assumed to be mutually dominant and referential. The source proposes inverting that assumption and letting the imagery rule — determining not only the project's overall compositional structure but the compositional and stylistic attributes of the type. Its reason is that typography is always a pattern of lines whereas images present a radically greater range of form languages, so applying an image's language to text quickly relieves a designer of presumptions about how text should behave and how layouts ought to be organised. Two directions are named: one in which typographic elements become in essence part of the imagery, and one in which the imagery sets up the logic for how type responds to it pictorially while the type retains its identity as a separate entity alongside the images.

mechanism.text: Type's form language is narrow — lines — so it cannot supply the variety a layout needs; imagery can, and letting it lead breaks the designer's default assumptions about text behaviour rather than arguing with them.

scope.conditions: projects that carry substantial image material

caveats.text: The source is explicit that the correspondence need not be literal: in one study the sizes, positions and radii of type arcs are not direct repetitions of any attribute in the image, and the mere fact of them is enough to create the visual connection. That weakens the method into a judgement call with no test.
Every instance is a layout this lane could not see. The two named directions are recorded because they are stated in words; the visual result of either is not inferred.

source_stated_problems: type and image are notoriously challenging to bring together; each has its own formal characteristics most often at odds with the other
source_stated_remedies: let the imagery determine the compositional structure and the type's compositional and stylistic attributes
either absorb the typographic elements into the imagery, or let the imagery set the logic to which separate type responds

The source adds that where attention moves between beats is itself specifiable: a subject placed with open look room toward one side sends the viewer's eye there, and the next beat should put its priority element where the eye was sent. item.label: how_a_still_image_carries_a_narrative_to_a_viewer_who_holds_the_code
item.description: Patel's chapter-4 account of poster meaning, assembled: the face opens attention before recognition; recognition of the star brings forward a persona that was built cumulatively by star, artist and public and is carried by a few fixed features; character types compress whole sets of relations into single figures so that the relations BETWEEN them are inferred rather than depicted; and because the code does the work, text can be minimised, which is what Indian posters in fact do.

whole_system_claim.text: A poster can carry a narrative structure it never depicts, provided the viewer holds the code. Attention is won by the face without recognition; meaning is then supplied by the viewer out of an accumulated persona and a familiar typology, not out of the poster. The poster's job is therefore indexing, not describing — which is why minimal text suffices and why the same design fails outside the code.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: Patel connects the first three members explicitly through her "hierarchy of responses" and her worked reading of the Deewaar poster. She does not present them as a model, does not draw the consequence for text as following from the type code, and never cites Dwyer's chapter-1 account of personification as the precondition. Assembling them into a causal chain, and adding those two members, is the extractor's. What the grouping ADDS, and what must be attributed to CANON-014, is the observation that all four devices fail together at the same boundary - the viewer who does not hold the code - which is visible across the set and not within any member.

dependencies.nature: the persona can only be indexed by a few features if personification, not impersonation, is the prevailing mode; Dwyer establishes that in chapter 1 and Patel relies on it in chapter 4 without restating it
text can be dropped only because the type code already carries the information text would have carried

tradeoffs.nature: Patel states the trade-off herself: designs that focus on one element are more universally understood but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. Reach and specificity are exchanged

item.source_warning_ref: Patel states that character types 'are not universally recognized' and are 'only fully understood by those with a knowledge of that culture' (printed p. 194); she draws the same boundary for star recognition at p. 183

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Moderate. The members are all Patel's, all from one chapter, and she does connect the first three explicitly through the "hierarchy of responses". What is the EXTRACTOR'S and must be attributed to CANON-014 is the addition of sk_dpci_0130 (minimal text) as a consequence of the code rather than as a separate observation, and the addition of sk_dpci_0080 (personification) from Dwyer's chapter as the precondition — Patel never cites Dwyer's chapter for this. The causal ordering is likewise the extractor's. The system is recorded as a reading of Patel's argument, not as a structure she sets out.

provenance.chapter: 4, Advertising and the Communication of Meaning (with one member from Ch. 1)
provenance.section: The Star Image; The Cultural Construction of Meaning; Character Types

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Patel's term for the layered way a poster is read: certain elements are immediately and universally understood while other elements require specific cultural knowledge to be understood.

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

INSPECTED: Figure 4.2, the premium-popular-discount construct, was opened. It is a schematic price-against-performance diagram showing the traditional line and three 'new offering' positions below it; it carries no data and is an illustration of the argument, not evidence for it

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Named cases without figures; a competing explanation for the same phenomenon appears elsewhere in the book unreconciled.

source_stated_problems: a shift in observed behaviour caused by a moving choice set is attributed to consumer character
source_stated_remedies: check whether the price-performance frontier moved before attributing a behaviour change to the buyer

positive: TVS Victor, a 125cc motorcycle offered at a 100cc popular price
Maruti Swift, a 'B' segment car with premium-category features

intra_source_relations.note: the segmentation being invalidated [relation re-expressed from the non-SPEC-03 'supported_by' by semantic review of this note]

provenance.section: THE BREAKDOWN OF THE PREMIUM-POPULAR-DISCOUNT CONSTRUCT OF MARKET STRUCTURE
provenance.locator: Ch. 4, section 'THE BREAKDOWN OF THE PREMIUM-POPULAR-DISCOUNT CONSTRUCT OF MARKET STRUCTURE'

item.question: Marketers observed richer consumers buying popular-segment products and called it down-trading. What does this source say was actually happening, and what is the general shape of the error?
item.answer: That the direction of the inference was wrong. The observation was read as a consumer trait — 'many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy' — and her correction is that 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', so the popular and discount segments in many cases now offered equivalent or better benefits at a lower price. She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced 'rogue' marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. Her instances are automotive — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B-segment car with premium features — and her conclusion is that 'the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant'. THE GENERAL SHAPE is attributing a change in observed behaviour to a change in the people, when what changed was the set of options they faced. Figure 4.2 was opened in this pass and carries no data: it is a price-against-performance schematic, so it illustrates the argument and is not evidence for it. No switching data is supplied anywhere.
item.support: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer'
item.confounders: Character explanations are attractive because they need no data and predict everything. This is the book's clearest instance, and its correction is also unmeasured.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Can your brand own something visual?' and 'Avoid style. Focus on substance.' (spine 15)
item.question: Sullivan endorses Krone's twenty-foot test and then makes a stronger claim of his own. State both, and identify the tension between this and his instruction to study a category's current visual conventions.
item.answer: Krone's requirement is a page style: you should be able to tell whose advertisement it is from a distance of twenty feet — and Sullivan notes what is interesting about it, which is that Krone was talking about print advertisements, not billboards. Sullivan's stronger claim is that the longer he is in the business the more convinced he is that art direction is where the major battle for brand building happens, because once a look is established and a design territory staked out, nobody else can use it without looking like your brand. He pairs it with an instruction to pull the look from the brand's own DNA rather than from current fashion, since riding every passing fad makes work trendy and derivative. The tension: knowing and avoiding a category's current clichés requires close attention to exactly the conventions this instruction says to ignore. He states both and does not reconcile them.
item.support: Krone is quoted from a 1968 trade interview; the stronger claim is Sullivan's own opinion, flagged by his phrasing, with no evidence. The colour-ownership examples are assertions about market perception with nothing measuring them. The tension is an extractor observation.
confounders: treating the twenty-foot test as calibrated; no viewing condition is specified
reading 'avoid style' as indifference to craft rather than as a warning against period fashion
assuming ownership of a colour or a look is established rather than asserted

source_terms: Using vernacular imagery or a vernacular compositional conceit imposes the look of something else onto a communication, embedding it in this new context, either to draw a comparison or, possibly, to comment on the subject being communicated
gestures of this kind often trade on forms associated with low culture, or undesigned visual experiences
item.claim: A further allusive strategy is to appropriate the visual language of common, everyday experience or the stylistic gestures associated with a particular context — the vernacular. Using vernacular imagery or a vernacular compositional conceit imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated; the source's example is an invitation to an exclusive art auction designed with the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. Because vernacular means the ordinary, gestures of this kind often trade on forms associated with low culture or with undesigned visual experience. The source dates the practice to Pop Art, citing Warhol's Brillo boxes and Rosenquist's paintings of spaghetti and household cleaning products.

mechanism.text: The borrowed look carries its origin's associations with it, so placing a subject inside it forces a comparison between the subject and the world the style came from. The gap between the two is the message.

scope.conditions: communications where a comparison with, or comment on, everyday culture is wanted

caveats.text: Vernacularism is defined by cultural reference and does not transfer between cultures. Hatch Show Prints signify the American Midwest, and Victorian illustrated books signify a small independent business, only to audiences who hold those associations.
The source treats the effect as reliable. It offers no case in which the borrowed style is simply read as the thing it was borrowed from.

source_stated_remedies: appropriate a visual language associated with ordinary experience to embed the subject in a new context

item.claim: Sullivan separates what changes from what does not and tells the maker to build on the second. Typefaces, design and art direction change; fads come and go. What people want — to look better, make more money, feel better, be healthy, and to have security, attention and achievement — he says is not likely to change. His instruction follows: direct the effort at those needs rather than at current visual affectations, and pull the look out of the brand's own DNA. He reports a consequence he says he noticed about simplicity specifically: it does not age, and the reduced advertisements in his simplicity chapter could be published tomorrow unchanged.

mechanism.text: Work anchored in a convention decays as the convention does; work anchored in a want that does not change has nothing to decay against. The observation about simplicity is the same argument in a stronger form — a piece with fewer elements has fewer places for a period style to attach.

scope.conditions: art direction decisions; the source does not claim style is irrelevant, only that it must not be the substance

caveats.text: the list of unchanging human wants is asserted, not derived, and reads as a mid-century motivational inventory
the timelessness observation is the source's own aesthetic judgement of his own selection of favourite advertisements, and he prefaces it with 'maybe it's just me'

item.claim: Sullivan holds that visual clichés are category-specific rather than general, and that the working procedure is therefore to go and learn which ones your category is using — visit the competitors' sites, watch their videos, study their social posts — and then not use those. He gives examples by category: grandfathers flying kites with grandchildren in insurance, earnest bespectacled people with a screen reflected in their glasses in technology. He calls the tired visual the picture version of low-hanging fruit, and prescribes the same clearing move: get them out of your system right away.

mechanism.text: A cliché is by definition the image the whole category already reaches for, so using it puts the brand inside the category's existing visual field rather than distinguishing it. This is the same accessibility argument he makes about early ideas: what is easily available to you is equally available to everyone working the same brief.

scope.conditions: art direction and concept selection within a defined competitive category

caveats.text: which images count as tired is judged by inspection and is time- and market-bound; the source's own examples are American category conventions of his period
the source separately endorses reusing established images that carry accumulated meaning (see sk_whip_0046), so the prohibition is on unmodified reuse, not on familiar imagery as such

item.question: This source denies that film clothing reflects real clothing while also insisting the audience brings a real-world grammar to it. How do both hold at once?
item.answer: They hold at different levels. The denial is about correspondence: 'the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions'. The insistence is about legibility: the audience brings a widely understood grammar of wearing the sari, with occasions requiring different saris by season, time of day and degree of formality, plus a colour code — red, green and yellow for festive occasions, white or pale for widows, black largely a Western fashion. The cinematic code is built ON that grammar without copying it. So the heroine almost invariably wore a sari as an emblem of chastity in contrast with the vamp, the unmarried heroine wears Western clothes before marriage and changes into salwar-khamees or a sari after it, and mothers and mother-figures always wear a sari. Real dress supplies the vocabulary; the films use it to mark moral and narrative position, not to record what people wore.
item.support: 'the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions'
item.confounders: Both halves are routinely dropped. Reading film dress as documentary evidence of period dress ignores the first; reading it as arbitrary costume design ignores the second.

source_terms: the name KamaSutra seemed particularly fortuitous to the agency team because it instantly satisfied three crucial requirements: maximum reach/intelligibility, an erotic connotation, and cultural legitimacy
item.claim: Reporting the anthropologist William Mazzarella, who reached the finding by speaking with the campaign's creators, the author records that the name "KamaSutra" was chosen for a condom brand because it satisfied three requirements at once: maximum reach and intelligibility, an erotic connotation, and cultural legitimacy. The brand was positioned against the government's Nirodh family-planning framing as an enabler of better lovemaking — "For the pleasure of making love" — and priced at a significant premium to both Nirodh and imported condoms.

mechanism.text: A taboo category cannot be addressed directly, so the name has to do three jobs at once: be understood by everyone, carry the charge the positioning needs, and supply a sanctioned cultural warrant that makes the charge admissible. A canonical indigenous text supplied all three where an invented or imported name would have supplied at most two.

scope.conditions: India, 1991, condom category, at a moment when the category's only mass framing was state family planning. The three requirements are stated for this case; the source does not claim they generalise.

caveats.text: the finding is Mazzarella's, an academic reporting interviews with the campaign team after the fact; it is a reconstruction of a naming decision, not a record made at the time

the campaign's outcome was contested: ASCI ordered modifications, a Rajya Sabha member sought a ban, Doordarshan withdrew its storyboard approval, and the company fell back to shop displays. Commercial success is not established by the source
generalising these three requirements into a naming checklist would be OUR extrapolation; the source presents them as a reconstruction of one decision

source_stated_problems: a category whose only available public framing is state health messaging cannot be premium-positioned inside that framing
source_stated_remedies: find a name that simultaneously supplies reach, the intended connotation, and cultural legitimacy

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Patel's term for the layered way a poster is read: certain elements are immediately and universally understood while other elements require specific cultural knowledge to be understood.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.
